lines.en: What makes a question philosophical is not that it has no answer, but that every answer opens ten more.
It is one thing to know the price of everything, and quite another to know the value of anything.
Were we certain that our choices are fully free, the question of responsibility would never arise.
However much we learn about the brain, the mystery of what it feels like to be someone remains.
Not until we face the possibility that we are wrong do we truly begin to think.
The unexamined life, said Socrates, is not worth living; but the over-examined life may be no easier.
It is argued that we do not see the world as it is, but as we are.
What the prisoner in the cave mistakes for reality is only the shadow of the world outside.
Little can be said for certain about justice, except that everyone demands it and few can define it.
Rarely does philosophy give us answers; what it gives us are better questions.
What the question 'why is there something rather than nothing' lacks in answers, it makes up for in depth.
It is strange that we demand meaning from the universe, yet never ask who told us it should have one.
Were our memories to be copied into another body, the question of which one is really 'us' would have no clean answer.
Not until we imagine being on the other side of our own rules do we test whether they are just.
However free we feel, our choices are shaped by a thousand influences we never notice.
